headline: Manage Hot Springs Access and San Juan National Forest Entry
reservation: While public forest access is generally open, private hot spring resorts often require advance soaking reservations to guarantee entry during peak winter and summer seasons. Accommodation in town is separate from amenity access; visitors should consult the San Juan National Forest office for any seasonal fire restrictions or backcountry permits required for the Weminuche Wilderness.

days.title: San Juan River and Thermal Waters

stops.name: The Great Pagosa Hot Springs
stops.detail: Observe the world's deepest geothermal aquifer from the public walkway before visiting a local bathhouse for a soak.

stops.name: San Juan River Walk
stops.detail: Follow the paved path through the heart of town to see the whitewater park and seasonal river activities.

days.driving: Minimal in-town transit; allow 15 minutes for local parking.
days.note: Soaking times are often limited during holiday weekends to manage capacity.

days.title: Continental Divide and High Alpine Vistas
days.start: Suggested: 8 AM from Hot Springs Blvd

stops.name: Wolf Creek Pass
stops.detail: Drive toward the Continental Divide for sweeping views of the San Juan Mountains and the Treasure Falls trailhead.

stops.name: Treasure Falls
stops.detail: Walk the short, steep trail to the base of this 100-foot waterfall located right off Highway 160.

days.driving: Allow 60–90 minutes roundtrip to the pass; conditions vary significantly with high-altitude weather.
days.note: Snow can linger on high-altitude trails well into June.

days.title: Chimney Rock Cultural Heritage

stops.name: Chimney Rock National Monument
stops.detail: Explore the Ancestral Puebloan archaeological sites set against dramatic twin rock spires.

stops.name: Piedra River Trail
stops.detail: Wander through the canyon for river views and potential wildlife sightings in a quieter forest setting.

days.driving: Allow 45 minutes to reach the monument; gravel access roads require careful navigation.
days.note: Check the monument website for seasonal gate closures and tour availability.

intel.title: Town Center and Trailheads
intel.text: Public parking near the San Juan River is plentiful but fills quickly on summer weekends. High-altitude trailheads like Williams Creek have limited space and may require early arrival.

intel.title: Mountain Connectivity
intel.text: Cellular service is reliable within Pagosa Springs city limits. Expect total signal loss once traveling east toward Wolf Creek Pass or into the Piedra River canyon.

intel.title: High Highway Logistics
intel.text: Gas stations are concentrated in Pagosa Springs and nearby Bayfield. Ensure a full tank before heading north into the remote forest access roads.

intel.title: Thermal Peak Hours
intel.text: Hot spring facilities are most crowded in the late afternoon and evening. Consider a morning soak for a more tranquil experience.

intel.title: Seasonal Road Closures
intel.text: Many Forest Service roads surrounding Pagosa Springs close for the winter and spring mud seasons. Always verify current gate status with the Pagosa Ranger District.

plan.arrival: Collect a vehicle at Durango La Plata County Airport and head east on US-160, stopping in Pagosa Springs for groceries before checking in.
plan.vehicle: A standard vehicle suffices for town, but a high-clearance 4WD is recommended for forest service roads; check rental contracts for unpaved road prohibitions.
plan.goldenHour: Reservoir Hill Park offers elevated views of the town and mountains during sunset, though clouds frequently obscure the horizon.
